title: Winnipeg woman spends weeks in hospital after surgery to treat chronic illness goes wrong

blocks.text: Manitoba

A Winnipeg nurse says she's spent more than three weeks at Health Sciences Centre after a surgery to treat her chronic illness left her with gaping wounds, necrotic tissue and an infection. Emma Cloney had a skin-excision surgery to help treat lipedema on Oct. 20.
Emma Cloney had a skin-excision procedure at Health Sciences Centre to help treat lipedema on Oct. 20
A Winnipeg nurse says she's spent more than three weeks at Health Sciences Centre after a surgery to treat her chronic illness left her with gaping wounds, necrotic tissue and an infection.

Emma Cloney, who has worked as a nurse at Manitoba's largest hospital, had a skin-excision surgery on her legs to help treat her lipedema — a chronic medical condition that causes painful fat buildup and swelling in a person's arms, legs and lower trunk area — on Oct. 20.
More than three weeks later, she was still in a hospital bed with severe wounds on her legs, dead skin tissue and an infection, she said.
"I've just been sitting with open wounds," Cloney said in an interview Thursday morning.
"I'm effectively bedbound because every time I try to walk, my wounds rip apart."

According to Lipedema Canada, there is no Canadian standard of care for the condition, which the advocacy group says affects about one in 10 women and other people assigned female at birth. Cloney is the advocacy group's president and co-founder.

She also lives with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a genetic condition that affects a person's connective tissues and can cause their skin to be stretchy and fragile. Someone with Ehlers-Danlos might have a difficult time healing wounds, with a risk of surgical incisions splitting open.

Cloney said the Oct. 20 surgery went well and she felt hopeful in the next few days. But then she developed "serious wound complications," including significant bruising and splintering along her leg wounds.

Cloney wants to be transferred out of the hospital so she can get hyperbaric oxygen therapy outside of Manitoba. The province confirmed Thursday evening that she will be moved. (Submitted by Emma Cloney)
Less than a week after the surgery, some of her tissue turned black and died, Cloney said.
Since then, she's been in the operating room several more times, while asking health-care providers at the hospital about different options that could help her heal.

"For a person with Ehlers-Danlos, delayed wound healing is really significant. And the longer I sit with open wounds, the more likely it is they'll develop a serious infection — an infection that could kill me," Cloney said, adding she developed an infection Wednesday.

She said she talked to providers about the possibility of getting hyperbaric oxygen therapy, where a patient goes into a pressurized chamber with 100 per cent oxygen. The Undersea and Hyperbaric Medical Society says it can help wounds heal and treat necrotizing soft tissue infections.
Cloney said she should be transferred to a hospital in Montreal because medical-grade hyperbaric therapy isn't available in Winnipeg.
She said a representative from Manitoba Health who handles out-of-province care called her Tuesday to say her transfer was approved. The wound became infected Wednesday, Cloney said.
"It's going to take a really long time to heal. Anything we can do to speed my wound healing and improve blood flow to those areas and prevent more damage, why wouldn't we be doing that?" she said.
"At this point, time is tissue."
Cloney says having Ehlers-Danlos syndrome complicates her ability to heal from surgery related to lipedema. (Submitted by Emma Cloney)

A Manitoba government spokesperson said in a statement sent to CBC News on Thursday evening that Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara's office has been in contact with Cloney. The spokesperson said Manitoba Health has approved one-time coverage for her out-of-province transportation and requested treatment.
After the approval, Cloney told CBC she wasn't told when her transfer would happen.

CBC also reached out to Shared Health, the health-care agency that oversees Health Sciences Centre, for comment. Several Manitoba government agencies saw disruptions to their email services Thursday amid a widespread Microsoft outage.

The Oct. 20 surgery was supposed to be Cloney's last in a series of 10 surgeries, with most of them being referred to medical teams in either the United States or Germany. While out of the country, she had specialized liposuction procedures for lipedema that aren't available in Canada.

blocks.text: Manitoba Health approved those out-of-province surgeries, but Cloney said she was told the skin-excision procedures could be done in Manitoba.

She said she would have preferred to stick with the team she's been working with in Germany, as they have specialized lipedema knowledge and understand how her other health conditions complicate her care.
Cloney believes she wouldn't be in her current situation had she been sent to Europe instead.
"They just don't have enough disease-specific knowledge to look after me [at HSC]. And I'm terrified, and I feel unsafe," she said.
Dr. Kaitlin Cyr, a Winnipeg-based family physician who specializes in obesity and lipedema, said there aren't many doctors across the country — let alone Manitoba — who can address the condition.

"There's very few physicians that have a good understanding of lipedema. And that really stems from the fact that it's not taught currently in our education system, in our medical schools or our residency programs," said Cyr, who is on the board of directors for Lipedema Canada.

blocks.text: She said care is getting better for non-surgical therapy for people with lipedema, such as compression garments or manual massage. But Canadians with the condition have to leave the country to receive high-volume liposuction procedures, as only cosmetic liposuction is offered here.
More education and training is needed to bridge that knowledge gap, Cyr said.
Cloney said the experience has shattered her trust with the staff at HSC and she wants to be transferred as soon as possible.
